title: Playing with Fire, Losing the Drive: Bidirectional Links Between Problematic Smartphone Use and Grit Dimensions
authors: Luming Zhao, Jiaxi Peng
abstract: This study examined bidirectional longitudinal associations between grit dimensions (consistency of interest [CI] and perseverance of effort [PE]) and problematic smartphone use (PSU) and tested cognitive flexibility as a mediating mechanism. A sample of 1,641 Chinese university students (55.2 percent female; Mage = 20.1 years) completed measures at two time points 6 months apart. A four-variable cross-lagged panel model revealed that CI and PSU negatively predicted each other over time, whereas PSU unidirectionally predicted decreased PE. Cognitive flexibility partially mediated the PSU-to-PE pathway (indirect effect = −0.004, 95 percent bootstrap CI [−0.010, −0.0001]). Competing models analysis confirmed this directionality: the forward mediation (PSU → cognitive flexibility → PE) was significant, whereas the reverse was not. These findings demonstrate that grit dimensions exhibit distinct longitudinal patterns with PSU and identify cognitive flexibility as a cognitive mechanism through which PSU specifically undermines effort persistence. Implications for dimensional approaches to grit and targeted interventions are discussed.

title: Who to activate next? Predicting influential and susceptible users in social media marketing with CFT-SIS
authors: Syrios Siyao Li, Sufang Wang, Yufei Wu, Yuanyuan Jamie Li, Matthew Kwok On Lee
abstract: Purpose The proliferation of online social networks (OSNs) has brought opportunities and challenges in managing marketing information flows. This study aims to develop an organization-level personalized monitoring model for marketing campaigns, which not only tracks the dynamics of information dissemination but also identifies influential, susceptible and cost-efficient participants to activate in the next round of campaigns. Design/methodology/approach This study develops a novel CFT-SIS framework that integrates curated flows theory (CFT) with the epidemiological susceptible-infected-susceptible (SIS) framework and differentiates information dissemination through broadcasting and narrowcasting channels. It combines users’ susceptibility with their historical influence in brand-specific campaigns to construct the influence-susceptibility index (ISI), precisely measuring both activation difficulty and resulting impact. Findings The CFT-SIS framework enables real-time monitoring of information diffusion by capturing both horizontal spread within individual campaigns and longitudinal interconnections across multiple campaigns. Compared to conventional SIS formulations, it demonstrates higher accuracy and stability in predicting user states. The proposed ISI effectively identifies dual-role users who are both highly influential and easily activated, enabling deeper propagation at lower cost and highlighting participants who drive sustained campaign success. Originality/value This study advances theoretical understanding of sustained social media marketing by identifying a novel and structurally emergent mechanism through which curation hierarchy reshapes user susceptibility and influence across network positions over time. In practice, the model enables the identification of high-impact, easily activated users, supporting more efficient campaign design and resource allocation in social media marketing.

title: Through their eyes: neural and behavioral evidence for enhanced immersion via point-of-view editing
authors: Moran Ovadia, Shiri Davidovitch, Romi Sion, Naama Shoham, Nimrod Keren, Sergei Freedman, Cynthia Cabañas, Dov Rubinstein, Mark A Thornton, Jonathan Frome, Liad Mudrik, Tim J Smith, Gal Raz
abstract: Point-of-view (POV) editing—the juxtaposition of a character’s gaze with the object of that gaze—is presumed to function as a unique empathic device that dissolves viewer-character boundaries; however, direct empirical evidence remains scarce. This study provides the first systematic functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral investigation into whether POV editing facilitates shared attention and intentionality. 39 adults viewed 8 original narrative movies containing POV sequences or closely matched control conditions. POV sequences increased fixation durations on characters’ faces and enhanced subsequent recognition of gazed-at content. Neurally, POV editing elicited stronger responses in regions implicated in mentalizing and increased shared, item-specific activation patterns across viewers within areas associated with perspective-taking and goal-directed control. Multivariate decoding further indicates that a character’s gaze induced more robust neural signatures of character identity on subsequent target elements. Together, these findings support a functional role for POV editing in promoting joint attention and shared intentionality in audiovisual messages.

title: When YouTube-Specific Content Feels Positive
authors: Min Jung Kim, Drew P. Cingel
abstract: Abstract: This paper examines the prospective associations among positive verbal and physical expressions in YouTube-specific content, children's parasocial relationships, the quality of their offline peer relationships, and parents' perceptions of YouTube's role in child development. We conducted a three-wave longitudinal survey combined with a content analysis of 97 parents with children aged four to 6. Using structural equation modeling (SEM), we found that positive verbal and physical expressions in YouTube-specific content at Year 1 were significantly associated with children's parasocial relationships at Year 2. Parasocial relationships at Year 2 were negatively associated with the quality of children’s offline peer relationships at Year 3 but positively associated with parents’ perceptions of YouTube in the same year. By linking expressive features in YouTube-specific content to children's parasocial relationships and subsequent peer relationship quality and parental perceptions, the findings provide insight into how media environments may shape early social development.

title: The Meanings of News: How U.S. Adults Think About the Word “News”
authors: Stephanie Edgerly, Ayse D. Lokmanoglu, Christopher M. Dobmeier, Nathan Walter
abstract: This study explores the immediate, top-of-mind meanings audiences hold about “news.” Inspired by recent audience-centric approaches in defining news, we adopt a schema framework to investigate mental representations of the news concept. Using a national probability survey of U.S. adults, we employ a thought-listing exercise combined with a network analysis. Our findings paint a complex picture of news and its meaning today. We identify six distinct news schemas (i.e., clusters of co-occurring words) that correspond to different audience demographics, political ideology, and news consumption. The findings underscore that news is a dynamic concept with implications for journalism scholarship and practice.

title: Hybrid Moderation in Practice: How Users, AI, and Professionals Judge Uncivil Comments
authors: Aviv Barnoy
abstract: Online platforms increasingly rely on hybrid moderation systems that combine automated triage with professional human review, yet little research compares how these actors judge the same real content in production-linked settings. This article examines uncivil online comments as a platform-governance problem by comparing three decision-makers: registered users, a platform AI system, and professional moderators. Using a secondary dataset from a US-based publisher comment environment, we analyze real comments spanning five moderation categories: Violence, Doxxing, Hate Speech, Sexual Explicitness, and Personal Attacks. The dataset combines production-stage AI workflow dispositions, professional moderators’ final adjudications, and ex-post survey judgments from 863 registered users, yielding 8,588 user-comment decisions. Results show that users chose to allow publication of roughly two-thirds of the uncivil comments and that their decisions aligned more closely with the AI system’s publish-and-moderate versus hold-and-moderate orientation than with professional moderators’ publish-versus-block decisions. Divergence was concentrated in specific categories and items, especially Hate Speech. Users’ justifications suggest that permissive decisions often relied on threshold reasoning, rejection of toxicity, or free-speech concerns, whereas restrictive decisions more often relied on direct violation labels. Demographic and engagement-based predictors explained little variance in alignment. The findings suggest that users, AI systems, and professional moderators should not be treated as interchangeable moderation tools: they operationalize different thresholds and may be suited to different governance functions.

title: Presumed media influence and support for social media bans: The roles of social and elite-based validation
authors: Sarah Geber, Anne Schulz, Mike S. Schäfer, Thomas N. Friemel
abstract: The study examines how presumed influences of social media on young people, as well as perceptions of how widely such beliefs are shared, shape support for social media bans. Extending the Influence of Presumed Influence (IPI) model, we introduce second-order presumed influences, defined as perceptions about how widely others presume media influences, and propose a mechanism of social validation. We additionally examine elite-based validation, referring to perceived beliefs of influential actors (i.e. scientists, politicians, and the media), as well as perceived social norms. Using survey data ( N = 1270) collected in the context of debates about a social media ban for minors under 16 in Switzerland, we find that stronger presumed influences predict support for a ban. While we find no support for social validation, the results point to the relevance of elite-related perceptions, particularly presumed scientific consensus. Perceived social norms of ban support emerge as an additional predictor of regulatory preferences.

title: The role of AI competencies: How do AI knowledge, skills, and attitudes shape users’ understanding and evaluation of explainable news recommendations?
authors: Chenyue Wang, Anne C. Kroon, Judith Möller, Claes H. de Vreese, Sophie C. Boerman
abstract: This study investigates how explanations in AI-driven news recommender systems (RS) influence user understanding, trust, and attitudes toward the RS, and whether these effects depend on individual differences in AI competence. An online experiment ( N = 754) was conducted in the Netherlands with a no-explanation condition as baseline. Results show that joint explanations significantly improved users’ objective understanding of the RS but had no consistent direct effects on perceived understanding, trust, or attitudes toward the RS. Exploratory structural equation modeling revealed an indirect pathway in which explanations enhanced objective understanding, which increased perceived understanding, subsequently fostering greater trust and more positive attitudes. Moderation analyses showed limited evidence for AI competence conditioning explanation effects, with small benefits concentrated among users with higher AI knowledge. Together, these findings suggest that explanations in news RS are not universally effective: their effects appear to operate primarily through cognitive mechanisms, while competence-related differences remain limited and selective.

title: Do WhatsApp news channels help users navigate the information environment? A field experiment on information-related attitudes
authors: Camila Mont’Alverne, Patrícia Rossini, Antonis Kalogeropoulos
abstract: Messaging applications have become central sources of news, especially in the Global South, raising concerns about the quality of information circulating in these spaces. This study examines how receiving news through WhatsApp channels shapes key information-related attitudes in Brazil, including misinformation belief, news fatigue, and media trust. In a pre‑registered experiment conducted in November/December 2024, 601 participants from multiple Brazilian states were asked to subscribe to either a regional news channel or a fact‑checking channel operated by Globo, the largest media group in Latin America. The results show that accessing news via WhatsApp does not alter more stable attitudes, such as belief in misinformation or trust. However, it does reduce news fatigue and increases engagement with news on WhatsApp. As news consumption shifts toward private messaging platforms, these findings suggest their value lies less in reshaping political attitudes and more in maintaining routine connections between audiences and journalism.

title: When scientists ‘Tok: Memetic communication and scientific information engagement in short video-based social media
authors: Jon Benedik Bunquin, Alex Segrè Cohen
abstract: TikTok has rapidly emerged as an influential platform for science communication, particularly among younger audiences. Its affordances encourage memetic communication—characterized by imitation, humor, and participatory storytelling—offering scientists novel ways to engage publics. Our study explores scientists’ use of memetic elements on TikTok and their associations with audience engagement. Drawing on social media logic and platform vernacular theories, we conducted a quantitative content analysis of 1025 science-related videos from 113 TikTok creators. Findings revealed widespread use of emotional and conversational language, but fewer videos incorporated reappropriated media or collectivist storytelling. Multilevel models showed that imitation and humor positively predicted likes, shares, comments, and views, whereas reappropriation negatively predicted engagement metrics. These results underscore the importance of aligning science communication strategies with platform-specific vernaculars. We discuss implications for public science engagement in digital, algorithmically driven environments, where visibility and audience trust increasingly depend on culturally resonant and participatory content.

title: Accuracy and Defense Motives: Exploring Types of Information Insufficiency in the Risk Information Seeking and Processing (RISP) Model
authors: Timothy K. F. Fung, Ho Man Leung, Po Yan Lai, Robert J. Griffin
abstract: This study reconceptualizes information insufficiency as a goal-contingent construct within the Risk Information Seeking and Processing model. In multifaceted risk contexts, individuals confront health threats alongside challenges to deep-seated values and beliefs, producing different judgmental demands within a single risk event. Survey data from 858 Hong Kong adults show two distinct forms of information insufficiency, one oriented toward accurate safety judgments and another toward defending deep-seated values and beliefs. Each form is associated with distinct patterns of information seeking and processing. This study demonstrates how multiple goal-based information insufficiencies operate within the same individual in response to different judgmental demands.

title: When Moral Appeals Backfire and Discourage the Adoption of Plant-Based Meat Alternatives
authors: Yuanke Zhou, Wanjun Li, Liudmila Tarabashkina, Zhiyuan Wang
abstract: Public campaigns use moral appeals to promote a plant-based meat diet, but such appeals can also backfire. We found that the animal welfare appeal prompted higher purchase intention only among individuals with lower meat attachment and was damaging among consumers with higher meat attachment, with meat attachment moderating the pathway from meat-related cognitive dissonance to the adoption of plant-based meat. The best strategy to appeal to consumers with higher meat attachment was a description that did not contain any messages. Our study clarifies when and why moral appeals may backfire when promoting plant-based meat, delineating the limits of their persuasiveness.

title: Revisiting the Communication Mediation Model in the Age of Social Media: Longitudinal Evidence From Climate Misinformation Responses in China
authors: Liang Chen, Xiaoming Liu, Lunrui Fu
abstract: The Communication Mediation Model (CMM) posits that media attention stimulates interpersonal discussion, which shapes attitudes and behaviors. Yet its assumptions of linear sequencing and universal applicability remain underexamined. In the era of social media, communication flows are increasingly reciprocal and socially embedded, and response behaviors such as misinformation correction and fact-checking represent new forms of media engagement rather than merely offline actions. Using a three-wave panel survey in China ( n = 499), this study revises the CMM in the context of climate change misinformation on social media by testing temporal pathways and audience heterogeneity. Results show that media attention stimulates interpersonal discussion, which in turn predicts correction, though these relationships unfold concurrently within a single time interval rather than following a staggered temporal order. Multigroup analysis reveals that public self-consciousness conditions pathway activation. Findings highlight how social media environments extend the behavioral scope of the CMM and complicate its assumed temporal order. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

title: Unpacking the Relationship Between Algorithmic Literacy and Misinformation: A Multidimensional Approach Using Two Sequential Studies
authors: Teresa Correa, Sebastián Valenzuela, Ingrid Bachmann, Nicolás Tobar Jorquera, Natalia Solís-Valdés, Isabel Pavez
abstract: Digital literacy is often proposed as a remedy for misinformation, yet empirical evidence regarding its effectiveness remains mixed. One reason for these inconsistencies lies in the multidimensional nature of both literacy and misinformation. This article focuses on algorithmic literacy, a distinct and increasingly central form of digital literacy in platform-mediated communication, and examines how its cognitive and behavioral dimensions relate to multiple facets of misinformation engagement. Drawing on two probabilistic survey studies conducted in Chile—a nationally representative face-to-face survey ( N = 1,200) and a random-digit-dial telephone survey of urban adults ( N = 2,265)—we analyze how cognitive (algorithmic awareness and knowledge) and behavioral (strategic actions to navigate algorithmic systems) dimensions of algorithmic literacy relate to perceived misinformation exposure, misinformation sharing, objective and subjective news knowledge, and knowledge miscalibration. Across both studies, a consistent pattern emerges: algorithmic literacy is more strongly associated with cognitive outcomes—especially perceived misinformation exposure and knowledge—than with behavioral outcomes like sharing. Higher algorithmic awareness consistently predicts greater perceived exposure, suggesting heightened recognition, while its link to sharing behavior is less consistent. These studies highlight the relevance of distinguishing cognitive from behavioral dimensions of literacy across different stages of misinformation engagement.

title: Anti-Elitism Gets the Views: Populist Communication and Popularity on German Political YouTube
authors: Lukas Erhard
abstract: YouTube has become a central venue for political communication, but systematic evidence of how parties employ the platform remains limited. This article examines how German political parties use YouTube and how populist rhetoric shapes engagement. We distinguish between anti-elitism and people-centrism and analyze their prevalence in party videos alongside their effects on video performance. We compile a dataset of official YouTube channels from all major German parties (2017–2025), apply automated transcription, and use a transformer-based model (PopBERT) to detect populist language. Video performance is assessed primarily through views, modeled with quantile regression and hurdle approaches to capture the likelihood of videos reaching the top tier and conditional effects among successful content. Our results show that the Alternative for Germany (AfD) far surpasses other parties in subscribers, video production, and engagement. Content analysis reveals that AfD channels contain markedly higher levels of anti-elitist rhetoric, while people-centrism appears more evenly distributed across the party spectrum. Quantile regression models show that anti-elitism is positively associated with engagement in the upper tail of the view distribution for all parties except the Free Democratic Party (FDP). Hurdle models further indicate that anti-elitism is associated with a higher probability of entering the top performance tier not only for the AfD but also for the Christian Democratic Union / Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), Left, and the Social Democratic Party (SPD). Results for people-centrism are weaker and less consistent. The study contributes to research on digital populism by showing that anti-elitist rhetoric, more than people-centrism, is associated with video success on YouTube across populist and nonpopulist parties.

title: Democratic Satisfaction and the Public Sphere
authors: Agustín Goenaga
abstract: Public debate is central to most theories of democracy, yet few cross-national studies have examined its association with democratic satisfaction. This article identifies three features of national public spheres – pluralism, information, and respect – and presents annual measures of these features for 175 countries from 2000 to 2020. Among electoral democracies, pluralism remained stable, but the quality of information and the respectfulness of debate tended to decline during that period. Using data from the European Social Survey and the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems, we find that higher levels of pluralism, information, and respect correlate with greater democratic satisfaction, even after controlling for other democratic institutions, various socio-economic factors, and past levels of satisfaction with democracy. Notably, respect remains associated with higher democratic satisfaction when controlling for the other features of the public sphere. These findings call for further research into the relationship between non-electoral components of democracy and political attitudes.

title: Can Authoritarian Electoral Propaganda Compete with the Opposition? Experimental Evidence from Russia
authors: Michael Rochlitz, Koen Schoors, Nikita Zakharov
abstract: We examine the effectiveness of electoral propaganda in an autocracy, using Russia as a unique setting. Exploiting the unexpected release of a pro-regime propaganda video about Vladimir Putin shortly before the presidential election, we conducted a field experiment by randomly promoting the video to voters via a telephone survey and measuring self-reported voting behaviour after the election. Our results show that the pro-regime treatment successfully mobilized offline media consumers to vote for Putin, but failed to persuade online media users, and even backfired among respondents dissatisfied with the regime. Using electoral statistics for all major Russian cities and instrumenting public interest in the propaganda video with rainfall, we find a positive, albeit moderate, causal effect of the video on Putin’s vote share. As an alternative treatment, we used a viral anti-corruption video by opposition leader Alexei Navalny, which consistently undermined regime support among both offline and online media consumers.

title: Online gendered violence and visibility in electoral autocracies: Evidence from multi-level elections in Türkiye
authors: Jungmin Han, Müge Finkel, Steven Finkel, Firat Duruşan, Erdem Yörük
abstract: Online platforms have become indispensable tools for political candidates to gain visibility, particularly for female candidates in electoral autocracies who often lack access to traditional networks, party hierarchies, and media platforms. We argue that online visibility, while a resource for female candidates, disproportionately exposes them to online violence that functions as a mechanism of political control, reinforcing patriarchal exclusion from the political sphere. Our analysis draws on more than three million tweets directed at 1,834 candidates across the 2023 parliamentary and 2024 local election campaigns in Türkiye, providing a rare opportunity to observe how these dynamics unfold at both the national and subnational levels. We find that while online visibility increases abuse for all candidates, the effect is markedly stronger for female candidates, who are disproportionately targeted across diverse forms of violence, including profanity, demeaning and ridiculing language, physical threats, and ethnic and religious hate speech. Moreover, our results suggest that in local elections, where candidates rely more heavily on personalized campaigns, increases in visibility are more strongly associated with female candidates’ exposure to online violence.

title: Beyond Single-Shot Designs: Repeated Treatments, Affective Polarization, and Democratic Norms
authors: Libby Jenke
abstract: Although theory and observational work suggest that affective polarization should shape citizens’ support for democratic norms, experimental tests of this causal claim largely find null effects. Most studies assume any impact would be immediate and rely on one-shot manipulations. Yet democratic norms are sticky; brief shifts in partisan feelings may be too weak or fleeting to move them. I therefore test whether repeated treatments over several waves of a survey shift affective polarization and, in turn, support for democratic norms. I find no significant first-stage effects: the treatments do not change respondents’ affective polarization, so repeated exposures do not cumulatively move it and downstream effects on norms cannot be identified. I conclude by considering why my findings differ from studies that report significant effects for similar treatments. Many experiments measure affective polarization as hostility toward the outparty, whereas this study and observational work conceptualize it as the gap between inparty and outparty evaluations.

title: When propaganda resonates
authors: Xiaoxiao Shen
abstract: Existing scholarship on propaganda in authoritarian regimes centers on whether it persuades or coerces. Within the persuasion camp, researchers have examined how factors such as message source, content, credibility, and audience demographics shape propaganda effectiveness. This study shifts attention to psychological needs. Drawing on evidence from China, it integrates multi‐round survey experiments, a virtual lab‐in‐the‐field experiment using a mobile news app developed by the author, text analysis of state media, and field interviews. The results show that propaganda appealing to the need to belong, the need to maintain self‐esteem, or the need to express core values is most effective among individuals for whom the corresponding need is particularly strong—but generalized propaganda, even when psychologically engaging, is not. The findings suggest that propaganda is most persuasive when targeted to stable psychological orientations rather than designed for broad consumption. These findings have implications for understanding how authoritarian regimes sustain public support: propaganda effectiveness depends not only on content or reach, but also on how closely its psychological appeals correspond to the stable motivational orientations of its audience. The shift in authoritarian communication strategies toward psychologically targeted appeals makes the mechanisms identified here increasingly relevant to understanding contemporary propaganda.

title: Racialization of the democratic peace in foundational embedding models
authors: Juho Kim
abstract: One of the most prominent theories in modern international relations is the democratic peace theory, which posits that democracies tend not to engage in armed conflicts with fellow democracies. Recently, Rathbun, Parker, and Pomeroy examined this effect at a microstructural level, performing surveys, computational studies, and meta-analysis. Of particular originality in their work was embedding analysis, which I review and offer a systematic critique of. Then, I propose a new and improved methodology that addresses its issues while leveraging foundational embedding models. My replication results agree with their findings that the democratic peace effect is racialized, that is, it is associated with racial and ethnocentric motivations. The findings offer a timely guide in conducting embedding analysis in political science research.

title: Applying Multiple Imputation to Improve Estimates from Web Surveys: An Alternative to the Pseudoweighting Method
authors: Yulei He, Katherine Irimata, Guangyu Zhang, Yan Li
abstract: To improve the timeliness of data products, survey researchers and practitioners have increasingly used web surveys and alike to collect information for population health research and dissemination. From the statistical inferential perspective, these data are often referred to as nonprobability samples due to the lack of a well-defined probability sampling structure, or they come from probability panel surveys yet are subject to high nonresponse and/or coverage errors. Certain statistical adjustments are therefore needed to make proper inferences using web surveys. With a high-quality reference probability survey available, one popular adjustment approach is to create pseudoweights that properly “weight” the web survey samples back to the target population underlying the reference survey in order to produce population-weighted estimates of the target of interest. When the variable of interest is collected in the web survey but not in the reference survey, the analytical question can also be framed as a missing data problem. Thus we propose to multiply impute the missing variable on the reference survey which combines the information from both data sources. We illustrate main features and performances of the multiple imputation strategy using a simulation study. The simulation results have shown that the multiple imputation analysis method is comparable to the pseudoweighting method, both of which can adequately account for the nonprobability feature of web surveys to improve the statistical inference. We also present a real data analysis based on the web-based Research and Development Survey and the interviewer-administered National Health Interview Survey. Our research shows that results from different imputation and pseudoweighting models can be compared to better understand features of the web survey data and improve the analysis.

title: Where You Are Is What You Get! Inconsistencies of Digital Trace Data across Download Locations
authors: Johanna Hölzl, Florian Keusch, John Collins
abstract: To collect digital trace data, researchers continue to rely on for-profit companies’ Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). These APIs often return samples of the data based on intransparent sampling procedures and algorithms. In this paper, we extend research on the reliability of digital trace data from APIs by examining the effect of the download location on inconsistencies across returned samples: Do we get different values from digital trace data APIs depending on where we download the data from? We compare samples from Google Trends, YouTube Data, and the New York Times (NYT) API from four countries across three continents (Austria, Germany, the U.S., and Australia) for the same query parameters (i.e., search term, region, and time range). Our results show that the download location impacts the returned samples for all three APIs, depending on the query. We find large inconsistencies for samples from Google Trends and the YouTube Data API, while the NYT API returns identical article sets from each download location for most queries. We conclude with practical recommendations for researchers using these APIs. Our findings serve as a cautionary reminder for social scientists relying on sampling-based APIs as they point to yet another limitation regarding their reliability and reproducibility.

title: The Threat of Analytic Flexibility in Using Large Language Models to Simulate Human Data
authors: Jamie Cummins
journal_full: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science
abstract: Social scientists are now using large language models to create “silicon samples”: synthetic data sets intended to stand in for human respondents. However, producing these samples requires many analytic choices, including model selection, sampling parameters, prompt format, and amount of demographic or contextual information provided. Across two studies, I examine whether these choices materially affect correspondence between silicon samples and human data. In Study 1, I generated 252 silicon-sample configurations for a controlled case study using two social-psychological scales, evaluating whether configurations recovered participant rankings, response distributions, and between-scales correlations. Configurations varied substantially across all three criteria and configurations that performed well on one dimension often performed poorly on another. In Study 2, I extended this analysis to a published silicon-sample use case by reexamining Argyle et al.’s Study 3 using 66 alternative configurations. Correlations between human and silicon association structures differed substantially across configurations, from r = .23 to r = .84. Taken together, the results from these studies demonstrate that different defensible configuration choices can materially alter conclusions about the fidelity of silicon samples. I call for greater attention to the threat of analytic flexibility in using silicon samples and outline strategies that researchers may adopt to reduce this threat.

title: Untrustworthy sources on Facebook and Instagram in 2020: Concentrated exposure but no attitudinal effects
authors: Olivier Bergeron-Boutin, Brendan Nyhan, Jaime Settle, Emily Thorson, Magdalena Wojcieszak, Taylor Brown, Adriana Crespo-Tenorio, Carlos Velasco Rivera, Hunt Allcott, Pablo Barberá, Drew Dimmery, Deen Freelon, Matthew Gentzkow, Sandra González-Bailón, Andrew M. Guess, Edward Kennedy, Young Mie Kim, David Lazer, Neil Malhotra, Devra Moehler, Jennifer Pan, Daniel Robert Thomas, Rebekah Tromble, Arjun Wilkins, Beixian Xiong, Chad Kiewiet de Jonge, Annie Franco, Winter Mason, Natalie Jomini Stroud, Joshua A. Tucker
abstract: Despite concern about exposure to content from untrustworthy sources on social media, little is known about the frequency or effects of exposure to their content. We examine 2020 data from all active US adults on Facebook and Instagram to measure exposure to content from Pages, groups, and web domains on Facebook and public accounts on Instagram that repeatedly publish misinformation. We find that average users saw relatively little content in their feeds from these untrustworthy sources; exposure was highly concentrated. A multimonth field experiment during the 2020 election among consenting users reduced feed-based exposure to content from untrustworthy sources by approximately 70% on both platforms but had no measurable effects on numerous preregistered outcomes, even among participants with high pretreatment exposure. Our results demonstrate that a feasible platform intervention can successfully reduce exposure to content from untrustworthy sources but suggest that these changes are unlikely to have immediate effects on attitudes and beliefs.
